notes.title: Chapter map: Stdlib & systems

headings.text: 🌳 How should this object cross a boundary?

notes.html:
The standard-library modules a service touches every day, each with one trap that only shows in production. These notes are mostly independent; read each arrow as a sentence: serialization used by multiprocessing.

Blue = SUPPORTING, yellow = BREADTH, grey = another chapter (dashed edges). No CORE notes: each is a module, not a mechanism.

Reading order:68 collections & heapq69 serialization70 filesystem & subprocess71 logging72 datetime & numerics

How should this object cross a boundary?

The serializers in 69 are alternatives, so the choice lives here (moved from note 69).

What each leaf is, and the one condition that would change the answer:

  • 🛂 json + schema (Pydantic): if the payload is huge and on a hot path, parse with model_validate_json straight from bytes rather than json.loads first.

  • json (serialization): if you start writing nested default= encoders, you've grown an untyped schema; switch to Pydantic.

  • 🗄️ database or schema'd format: if the data is a short-lived cache entry you can rebuild, pickle is fine; it's durability that rules it out.

  • pickle (serialization): if the bytes ever travel through a queue another team can write to, go back to the first question: it's untrusted now.

  • The one big idea: each module's dangerous default is the convenient one: shell=True, utcnow(), pickle.loads, f-strings in log calls, float for money. The safe form is one argument or one constructor away.

  • The two most-confused pairs: naive vs aware datetime (72: comparing them raises TypeError) · pickle vs json (69: reconstruction instructions vs a photograph of six types).

  • Ten minutes before an interview: 69's hostile-pickle sequence diagram, 72's UTC pipeline, then this tree.

  • Cross-chapter: list internals (why deque exists) · multiprocessing (pickle is its wire format) · structured logging (where 71 goes in production).

notes.title: collections & heapq
notes.html:
References

collections: container datatypes · heapq: heap queue algorithm

TL;DR

defaultdict for grouping, Counter for counting, deque for O(1) at both ends, heapq for a min-heap on a plain list. Push heap entries as (priority, counter, item): ties compare the next element.

Recall

Prompt Answer
deque vs list for a queue? deque is O(1) at both ends; list.insert(0) / pop(0) shifts every element (list internals).
Is OrderedDict obsolete since 3.7? Mostly: dict keeps insertion order. OrderedDict still has move_to_end and order-sensitive ==.
The heapq tuple gotcha? Equal priorities compare the payload: two dicts raised TypeError: '<' not supported.

The idea

defaultdict(list) removes the check-then-insert dance from grouping code. Counter is a multiset (most_common()). deque is the queue and sliding-window primitive: on CPython 3.12 a push and pop at the front of a 100,000-item list took 25 µs, against 28 ns for deque, and maxlen makes it a ring buffer that evicts the oldest. heapq keeps a list in min-heap order: O(log n) push and pop, O(1) peek, the engine under schedulers and nsmallest. OrderedDict survives for hand-rolled LRUs, and because OrderedDict(a=1, b=2) == OrderedDict(b=2, a=1) is False while the plain-dict version is True.

Code

from collections import defaultdict, deque
import heapq, itertools
groups = defaultdict(list)
groups["retry"].append("job-7")          # a missing key builds the list
window = deque(maxlen=3)
for i in range(5): window.append(i)      # → deque([2, 3, 4], maxlen=3)
h, tie = [], itertools.count()
heapq.heappush(h, (2, next(tie), {"name": "low"}))
heapq.heappush(h, (1, next(tie), {"name": "urgent"}))
print(heapq.heappop(h)[2])               # → {'name': 'urgent'}: smallest tuple first

notes.title: Serialization (pickle, json, marshal)
notes.html:
References

pickle · json · marshal

TL;DR

pickle stores reconstruction instructions for almost any object graph, so unpickling untrusted bytes is remote code execution. json is safe and interoperable but knows six types; marshal is CPython's private .pyc format, for nothing else.

Flow:pickle.dumps(obj)classes and functions recorded by import path, state by __dict__ or __reduce__bytes travelpickle.loads runs a small stack machinere-imports each named callable and calls itobject rebuilt (or, from a stranger, whatever they named runs)

Recall

Prompt Answer
The pickle security rule? Unpickling calls whatever the payload names (__reduce__): never unpickle untrusted bytes. Validation can't fix it.
What can't json represent? Sets, tuples (they come back as lists), bytes, datetimes, custom classes, non-string keys ({1: "a"} became {"1": "a"}).
Where does pickle cost you invisibly? Multiprocessing: every argument and result is pickled per call.

The idea

A pickle isn't a data snapshot; it's a program. On CPython 3.12:

import os, pickle
class Evil:
    def __reduce__(self):
        return (os.system, ("echo PWNED-during-load",))  # "rebuild me by calling this"
blob = pickle.dumps(Evil())
pickle.loads(blob)        # prints PWNED-during-load, then returns 0

The command ran during loads, before any object existed to inspect. That's the documented extension mechanism, not a bug, so "we validate after loading" is too late by definition. The same design explains every pickling error: functions and classes are stored by qualified name and re-imported at load, so a lambda (PicklingError: Can't pickle <function <lambda>>) has no name to store, and a socket (cannot pickle 'socket' object) is kernel state, meaningless in another process.

The trade: pickle round-trips almost any Python object graph, cycles included, and in exchange the bytes can execute code and are coupled to your class names.

How it works

What loads actually does with a hostile payload:

Rule What actually happens
By name, not by code myapp.models.User is written as an import path; rename the class and every stored pickle breaks with AttributeError or ModuleNotFoundError.
State The instance __dict__ (or __getstate__'s result), pickled recursively with memoization, which is how cycles survive.
Mitigations Sign the channel (HMAC), or restrict Unpickler.find_class to an allowlist; the honest default for untrusted input is not pickle.
Protocols Protocol 5 (3.8+) adds out-of-band buffers for large arrays. DEFAULT_PROTOCOL is 4 on 3.12 and 5 on 3.14; readers must be at least as new.

Code

One object, two boundaries:

import json, pickle
from dataclasses import dataclass, asdict
from datetime import datetime, timezone

@dataclass
class Event:
    name: str
    at: datetime

e = Event("deploy", datetime(2026, 10, 2, 9, 0, tzinfo=timezone.utc))

# untrusted or cross-language boundary: explicit encoding
wire = json.dumps(asdict(e), default=lambda o: o.isoformat())
# → {"name": "deploy", "at": "2026-10-02T09:00:00+00:00"}   (a string comes back)

# trusted internal hop, e.g. our own task queue: the real object round-trips
blob = pickle.dumps(e, protocol=pickle.HIGHEST_PROTOCOL)
type(pickle.loads(blob).at)      # → datetime, ONLY safe because we produced blob

Nested default= lambdas grow into an untyped shadow schema; at real API boundaries that's Pydantic's job.

Interview

30-second answer: Three serializers, three contracts. pickle handles nearly any object graph by recording reconstruction instructions, which is exactly why unpickling untrusted data is remote code execution: __reduce__ can name any callable. json is safe, interoperable and readable, but limited to six types, so everything else needs explicit encoding. marshal is CPython's private, version-unstable .pyc format. Pickle for trusted internal hops only; json or a schema at every boundary.

Q · Mechanism — What decides whether an object is picklable, and why do lambdas and sockets fail? Pickle stores classes and functions by qualified name and re-imports them at load, plus instance state from __dict__ or __getstate__. So both sides need compatible code, and anything without an importable name fails: lambdas and classes defined inside functions. Sockets, file handles, locks and DB connections fail because they're kernel state; objects holding them need __getstate__/__setstate__ to drop and re-establish them. That's also why multiprocessing with spawn rejects lambda targets.

Compare

pickle json marshal
Coverage almost any object graph, cycles six types; the rest is your encoder code objects, primitives
Untrusted input arbitrary code execution worst case a big or deep payload can crash the interpreter
Cross-language, readable no, no yes, yes no, no
Stable across versions protocols yes; your classes are the risk universal no: changes per release
Use for trusted IPC, task queues, caches APIs, config, logs nothing (CPython's own .pyc)

Pitfalls

  • "Pickle is unsafe like eval; I can sanitize it"
    The unsafety is the feature: reconstruction calls what the payload names.
    ↳ Fix: an allowlisted find_class, a signed channel, or not pickle.
  • "If dumps succeeded, loads works anywhere"
    Dumps records import paths; a rename or a missing module breaks every stored blob.
    ↳ Classic: the broken cache after a deploy.
  • Never pickle across a trust boundary.
    ↳ Includes: user uploads, other teams' services, any message bus you don't fully control.
  • Don't pickle long-lived data for durable storage.
    ↳ Why: bytes are coupled to class definitions; a refactor strands them. Use a database or a schema'd format.
  • Don't ship big arrays through default pickling in multiprocessing.
    ↳ Why: per-call serialization can exceed the compute; use shared memory or protocol 5 buffers.
  • 🔖 Version: protocol 5 3.8+ (PEP 574); DEFAULT_PROTOCOL 4 through 3.13, 5 from 3.14; json's six-type limit is permanent by design.
    ↳ Note: checked on CPython 3.12.13 and 3.14.6.

Connections

Path:import systemserializationmultiprocessing
  • Builds on the import system: pickle stores qualified names and re-imports them at load.
  • Used by multiprocessing: pickle is the IPC wire format, and its cost decides what parallelizes.
  • Contrasts with Pydantic: a schema-first answer to json's six types, safe on untrusted input.
  • Used by custom exceptions: exceptions crossing processes must pickle.
  • Same idea elsewhere: Java deserialization (ObjectInputStream) has the same gadget-chain RCE class, for the same reason.

notes.title: Filesystem & Subprocess
notes.html:
References

pathlib · subprocess

TL;DR

pathlib.Path joins with / and reads, writes and globs as methods; no string surgery. subprocess.run([...], check=True, capture_output=True, timeout=…) with a list of arguments: no shell, no injection, no pipe deadlock.

Recall

Prompt Answer
The shell=True trap? The string goes through a shell: interpolated input becomes shell injection. Pass a list, shell=False.
The pipe deadlock? The child fills a full PIPE while the parent wait()s: both block. run() and communicate() drain both pipes.
Path("etc") / "app"? __truediv__ overloaded for joining, with the OS's separator.

The idea

shell=True hands your string to a second interpreter whose grammar gives ;, $() and | meaning. On CPython 3.12, name = "x; echo INJECTED" passed through f"echo {name}" with shell=True printed x and then ran the injected echo INJECTED; ["echo", name] printed x; echo INJECTED as one harmless argument. The other trap is silence: without check=True, a nonzero exit returns normally, which is how a failed backup passes CI. With it, run(["false"], check=True) raised CalledProcessError: … returned non-zero exit status 1. timeout= kills a hung child, and mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True) is idempotent, with no exists() race.

Code

from pathlib import Path
import subprocess
cfg = Path.home() / ".config" / "app"            # an object, not string concatenation
cfg.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)           # idempotent
r = subprocess.run(
    ["pg_dump", "--dbname", db_url],             # LIST of args: no shell, no injection
    capture_output=True, text=True,              # drains both pipes: no deadlock
    check=True, timeout=300,                     # nonzero exit RAISES; a hung child is killed
)
(cfg / "backup.sql").write_text(r.stdout, encoding="utf-8")

notes.title: Logging
notes.html:
References

Logging HOWTO · logging

TL;DR

Loggers form a tree by dotted name; records propagate up to root, where handlers (destination) and formatters (rendering) live. Libraries only call getLogger(__name__); the application configures handlers once, at the entry point.

Recall

Prompt Answer
Logger vs handler vs formatter? Logger: a named emit point in a tree. Handler: a destination. Formatter: the rendering.
The library logging rule? Libraries add no handlers; only the application configures them, once.
Why are f-strings in log calls wrong? log.debug(f"{x}") formats even when DEBUG is off; log.debug("%s", x) defers it.

The idea

getLogger(__name__) makes the logger tree mirror your package layout, so levels can be tuned per module, and records propagate to root, where one configuration decides where and how they go. Code decides what to say; the entry point decides where. On CPython 3.12 with the level at INFO, log.debug(f"{obj}") still called obj.__str__(), while log.debug("%s", obj) never did: deferred formatting is free when a level is off, and keeps arguments as separate fields for structured handlers. Production logs are JSON lines queried by machines, with request_id carried across async boundaries by context variables (structured logging).

Code

import logging
log = logging.getLogger(__name__)                 # module level; tree = package path

def charge(user_id: str, cents: int):
    log.info("charge started user=%s amount=%d", user_id, cents)  # deferred formatting
    try:
        ...
    except PaymentError:
        log.exception("charge failed user=%s", user_id)   # ERROR level + traceback
        raise                                              # log-and-raise only at boundaries

# entry point ONLY, never in library code:
# logging.basicConfig(level=logging.INFO)   # real apps: dictConfig with a JSON formatter

notes.title: Datetime & Numerics Gotchas
notes.html:
References

datetime · zoneinfo · Floating-point arithmetic: issues and limitations · decimal

TL;DR

Store and compute time as aware UTC; attach a ZoneInfo only for display, or when the requirement really is wall-clock time. Floats are binary, so 0.1 is already inexact: compare with math.isclose, do money in Decimal("…") or integer minor units.

Flow:a datetime arrivesnaive? attach the known source zoneconvert to UTC: store, order and compute hereconvert to the viewer's ZoneInfo at displaya number arrivesmoney? Decimal from a string, or int paisemeasurements? float + isclose

Recall

Prompt Answer
Naive vs aware datetime? Aware carries tzinfo; naive is a wall-clock reading. Comparing the two raises TypeError.
Why is datetime.utcnow() a trap? It returns a naive datetime that only implies UTC; deprecated since 3.12. Use datetime.now(timezone.utc).
Why does 0.1 + 0.2 != 0.3? Binary floats can't represent 1/10; each literal is the nearest double, and sums round again.

The idea

Two families of "works in the demo, breaks in prod". On CPython 3.12:

datetime.utcnow().tzinfo                 # → None, plus a DeprecationWarning
datetime.utcnow() < datetime.now(timezone.utc)
# → TypeError: can't compare offset-naive and offset-aware datetimes
0.1 + 0.2                                # → 0.30000000000000004
Decimal(0.1)                             # → 0.1000000000000000055511151231257827021181583404541015625

utcnow()'s UTC-ness lives only in your head, so the first mix with an aware value fails or, worse, gets serialized and the reader guesses the zone. The float error is in the representation: 0.1 is rounded at parse time, before any arithmetic, and Decimal(0.1) faithfully preserves that wrong double, which is why Decimal must be built from strings.

The trade: aware UTC and base-10 money types cost a little ceremony at the edges, and in return ordering, DST and rounding stop being silent bugs.

How it works

Rule What actually happens
DST: elapsed vs wall-clock From 09:00 on 7 Mar 2026 in New York, UTC + 24 h converted back gave 10:00 local (spring-forward); + timedelta(days=1) in the local zone gave 09:00, only 23 h later. Pick the one the requirement means.
Gaps and folds Some local times don't exist (spring) and some happen twice (autumn); fold=0/1 picks which. Naive values can't express this.
Base 2 A float is a 53-bit significand × 2ⁿ, exact only for m/2ⁿ. 1/10 has a factor of 5, so it repeats forever in binary and is truncated.
Decimal and Fraction Decimal is base 10 with set precision and explicit rounding (ROUND_HALF_EVEN gave 2.5 → 2); Fraction is exact ratios, unbounded and slow.

Code

from datetime import datetime, timezone
from zoneinfo import ZoneInfo
from decimal import Decimal, ROUND_HALF_EVEN
import math

created = datetime.now(timezone.utc)                  # aware UTC, never utcnow()
ist = created.astimezone(ZoneInfo("Asia/Kolkata"))    # zone only at the display edge

price = Decimal("199.99")                             # STRING constructor
gst = (price * Decimal("0.18")).quantize(Decimal("0.01"), rounding=ROUND_HALF_EVEN)
# → Decimal('36.00'): explicit rounding, banker's rule, unbiased over many rows

assert 0.1 + 0.2 != 0.3                               # binary base, not a bug
assert math.isclose(0.1 + 0.2, 0.3)                   # the right float comparison

Decimal arithmetic measured ~50 ns against ~8 ns for the same float expression on 3.12: fine for ledgers, wasteful for ML and metrics, where data was never base-10 exact. For money at scale, integer minor units (paise, cents) are exact, fast and database-friendly.

Interview

30-second answer: Time: store and compute in aware UTC with datetime.now(timezone.utc), and convert with zoneinfo only at display; naive datetimes hide an assumption that breaks at the first DST change or cross-region deploy, and utcnow() is the deprecated trap that looks right. Numbers: floats are binary, so 0.1 is already inexact: math.isclose for comparison, Decimal from strings or integer minor units for money.

Q · Mechanism — Why can't binary floating point hold 0.1, and what do Decimal and Fraction fix? A double represents exactly the values m/2ⁿ with a 53-bit m. 1/10 has a 5 in its denominator, so it's an infinite binary expansion truncated at parse time: 0.1 is stored as 0.1000000000000000055…, and every operation rounds again, so 0.1 + 0.2 lands on a different double than 0.3. Decimal moves to base 10 with explicit precision and rounding modes, but only exact if built from a string. Fraction keeps integer ratios: exact, unbounded, slow.

Compare

float Decimal Fraction int minor units
Exact for powers of two base-10 decimals at set precision all rationals whole paise or cents
Speed hardware, fastest ~6× slower here slowest, grows unbounded hardware int
Rounding IEEE, fixed explicit modes never rounds written once, at display
Reach for it science, ML, metrics money with fractional rates exact ratio math money at scale

Pitfalls

  • "utcnow() gives me a UTC datetime"
    It gives a naive one; mixing it with aware values raises TypeError.
  • "A literal like 0.1 is stored exactly; errors come from arithmetic"
    The error is in the representation, and Decimal(0.1) preserves it.
  • Don't compare floats with == after any arithmetic.
    ↳ Fix: math.isclose, or pytest.approx in tests.
  • Don't store local time with a zone when UTC works.
    ↳ Why: ordering, range queries and dedup get harder; the zone belongs to the viewer.
    ↳ Exception: future civil events ("9 am on-site"), where wall time is the contract.
  • Don't measure durations with time.time().
    ↳ Why: the wall clock steps under NTP; time.monotonic() is the duration clock.
  • 🔖 Version: zoneinfo 3.9+ (before it, pytz's different localize() API); fold 3.6+; utcnow() deprecated 3.12.
    ↳ Note: checked on CPython 3.12.13.

Connections

Path:is vs ==datetime & numericsserialization
  • Contrasts with is vs ==: float == compares exact bits, which after arithmetic is rarely what you mean.
  • Used by serialization: datetimes are json's most common gap; ISO format with an offset is the wire convention.
  • Used by testing: pytest.approx, frozen clocks and time-zone matrix tests pin these down.
  • Same idea elsewhere: Java's Instant vs ZonedDateTime and BigDecimal split time and money the same way.
